rationale: A wins because it treats missing facts as kill switches, not decoration. Its "Warby Parker says store shoppers spend more than online buyers. It will not say how much." is exactly the pressure-test angle; B's "Warby Parker is testing whether a pharmacy aisle sells glasses better than its own stores" invents a comparative test the update never gave. That is the difference between a pitchable angle and a tidy hallucination.
gaps_in_A: "Warby Parker built its brand on skipping the middleman" imports DTC brand history not supplied in the update; the channel angle works without that borrowed mythology.
"The company that made direct-to-consumer eyewear a category" is an unsupported category-history claim. Do not smuggle Wikipedia into a blind fact block.
"It will not say how much" is sharper than the facts allow; the update lacks the retail spend differential, but does not prove Warby refused to provide it.
"Story type: funding-mechanics" is mislabeled. This is capital allocation and disclosure scrutiny, not a funding story.
gaps_in_B: "Warby Parker bets its future on the stores it was built to disrupt" overstates both "future" and "built to disrupt"; neither is in the update.
"made its name proving glasses didn't need a showroom" and "online-first thesis Warby itself popularized" are outside facts presented as if the prompt supplied them.
"testing whether a pharmacy aisle sells glasses better than its own stores" is a flat invented comparison. The update says only that Warby is piloting pharmacy-chain distribution.
"CVS-MinuteClinic-style trend" plus "LensCrafters, Costco Optical" imports a trend and competitor frame without source support. Context is useful; unsourced scenery is still scenery.
